question: In a head-on meeting situation between two power-driven vessels, what does the Navigation Rules require of both operators?
choice_a: Each vessel should alter course to starboard (right) so that they pass port-to-port, like cars on a road
choice_b: Both vessels should stop dead in the water and wait for radio instructions
choice_c: Only the smaller vessel needs to alter course
choice_d: Both vessels should turn to port (left) to pass starboard-to-starboard
explanation: In a head-on meeting situation, the Navigation Rules direct both power-driven vessels to alter course to starboard so they pass each other port side to port side, similar to the convention of keeping right on a roadway.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, head-on meeting)

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the 'stand-on' vessel that should hold its course and speed?
choice_a: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching on its own starboard (right) side
choice_b: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching on its own port (left) side
explanation: In a crossing situation, the vessel that sees the other approaching from its own starboard side is the 'give-way' vessel and must take early, obvious action to avoid collision; the vessel with the other approaching on its port side is the 'stand-on' vessel and should generally hold course and speed unless collision becomes imminent.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, crossing situation)

question: What must the 'give-way' vessel do in a crossing or overtaking situation?
choice_a: Speed up to cross in front of the other vessel as quickly as possible
choice_b: Maintain its exact course and speed regardless of risk
choice_c: Take early and substantial action to keep well clear of the other vessel, such as slowing, stopping, or altering course
choice_d: Sound five short blasts and continue on the same course
explanation: The give-way vessel must take early, obvious action -- well before a close-quarters situation develops -- to keep clear of the stand-on vessel, such as slowing down, stopping, or altering course.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, give-way vessel obligations)

question: In an overtaking situation, which vessel must keep clear of the other?
choice_a: The vessel being overtaken must always yield to the faster vessel
choice_b: Neither vessel has an obligation to yield in an overtaking situation
choice_c: The slower vessel must speed up to avoid being overtaken
choice_d: The vessel that is overtaking (coming from behind) must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken
explanation: The overtaking vessel -- approaching another vessel from more than 22.5 degrees abaft its beam -- is always the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken, which remains the stand-on vessel until well clear.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, overtaking situation)

question: In general right-of-way hierarchy, which of these vessels typically has priority over a stand-on power-driven vessel operating normally?
choice_a: A vessel not under command, restricted in its ability to maneuver, or a vessel engaged in commercial fishing with gear deployed
choice_b: A personal watercraft, which always has priority over every other vessel
choice_c: A vessel simply because it is painted a bright color
choice_d: Any vessel that arrived at the area first, regardless of type
explanation: The general right-of-way hierarchy gives priority to vessels with the least maneuverability or that are constrained by their work, such as vessels not under command, vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver, and vessels engaged in commercial fishing with gear deployed -- these vessels generally outrank an ordinary power-driven vessel operating under normal conditions.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (Navigation Rules right-of-way hierarchy)

question: Under the Navigation Rules, how does a power-driven vessel generally relate to a sailing vessel under sail alone?
choice_a: The sailing vessel must always give way to any power-driven vessel
choice_b: The power-driven vessel is generally the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the sailing vessel
choice_c: Sailing vessels have no right-of-way status under the Navigation Rules
choice_d: Right-of-way between sail and power depends only on which vessel is larger
explanation: As a general rule, a power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of a sailing vessel operating under sail alone, since sailing vessels have less maneuverability and cannot simply throttle up to avoid a collision -- though a sailing vessel overtaking a power-driven vessel becomes the give-way vessel.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, sail vs. power)

question: What sound signal does one short blast of a horn mean when power-driven vessels are meeting or crossing in sight of one another (U.S. Inland Rules)?
choice_b: I am anchored and at risk of dragging
choice_c: I intend to leave you on my port side / I am altering course to starboard
explanation: Under the U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, one short blast signals an intention to alter course to starboard (leaving the other vessel to port); two short blasts signals an intention to alter course to port, and three short blasts means the vessel is operating astern propulsion.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, sound signals)

question: What does five (or more) short, rapid blasts of a horn mean under the Navigation Rules?
choice_b: A signal that the vessel is about to anchor for the night
choice_d: A danger or doubt signal, warning that the intentions of another vessel are unclear or that a collision risk exists
explanation: Five or more short, rapid blasts is the danger/doubt signal, used when a boater does not understand another vessel's intentions or believes the other vessel is not taking sufficient action to avoid collision.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, danger signal)

question: What obligation does the Navigation Rules place on every vessel operator regarding lookout, regardless of right-of-way status?
choice_a: Maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing at all times, using all available means appropriate to the conditions
choice_b: Only the stand-on vessel needs to keep a lookout
choice_c: A lookout is only required at night
choice_d: Lookout duty may be skipped if radar or GPS is aboard
explanation: Every vessel, regardless of whether it is the stand-on or give-way vessel, must maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing at all times to accurately assess collision risk -- radar and GPS supplement, but never replace, an alert visual lookout.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (Navigation Rules, lookout requirement, Rule 5)

question: What is 'safe speed' under the Navigation Rules, and why does it matter on busy Missouri lakes?
choice_a: The maximum speed the engine is capable of producing at all times
choice_b: A speed at which a vessel can take proper and effective action to avoid collision and can be stopped within a distance appropriate to the prevailing circumstances, such as traffic density, visibility, and maneuverability
choice_c: A fixed speed of exactly 5 mph regardless of conditions
choice_d: A speed that applies only at night
explanation: Safe speed is not a single fixed number; it depends on visibility, traffic density, the vessel's maneuverability and stopping distance, and other prevailing conditions -- on a crowded Missouri reservoir on a summer weekend, safe speed may be well below what open, empty water would allow.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (Navigation Rules, safe speed, Rule 6), applied to Missouri lake traffic conditions

question: How should vessels normally pass each other in a narrow channel or fairway?
choice_a: Each vessel should hug the center of the channel regardless of oncoming traffic
choice_b: The larger vessel always has the right to occupy the center of the channel
choice_c: Each vessel should keep to the starboard (right) side of the channel as far as safe and practicable
choice_d: Vessels should travel in the middle and pass on whichever side is more convenient
explanation: In a narrow channel or fairway, vessels should keep to the starboard side as far as is safe and practicable, and a vessel should avoid crossing a channel in a way that impedes traffic that can only navigate safely within that channel.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (Navigation Rules, narrow channel rule, Rule 9)

question: What light must a vessel anchored outside a designated anchorage area on Missouri waters display from sunset to sunrise?
choice_a: No light is required for an anchored vessel under any circumstance
choice_c: A green light on the bow only
choice_d: A white all-round anchor light visible from all directions, so approaching vessels can see and avoid the anchored boat in the dark
explanation: A vessel anchored outside a designated anchorage must display a white, all-round anchor light visible from every direction between sunset and sunrise, warning other vessels of its stationary position in the dark.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (Navigation Rules, anchor light requirement, Rule 30)

question: What sound signal must a power-driven vessel underway sound at intervals of no more than two minutes in conditions of restricted visibility, such as fog?
choice_c: No sound signal is required in fog if the vessel has GPS
choice_d: Three short blasts followed by silence for the rest of the trip
explanation: In restricted visibility, a power-driven vessel making way must sound one prolonged blast at intervals of no more than two minutes, alerting nearby vessels to its presence when it cannot be seen -- a different, longer signal than the short blasts used for meeting, crossing, or overtaking maneuvers.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (Navigation Rules, restricted-visibility sound signals, Rule 35)

question: When two sailing vessels under sail alone are approaching each other and risk collision, which one is generally the stand-on vessel?
choice_a: The larger sailing vessel is always the stand-on vessel regardless of wind direction
choice_b: The vessel with the wind on its port side must keep clear of the vessel with the wind on its starboard side
choice_c: Sailing vessels have no right-of-way rules between each other
choice_d: Whichever sailing vessel is moving faster is automatically the stand-on vessel
explanation: Between two sailing vessels, the general rule is that the vessel with the wind on its port side gives way to the vessel with the wind on its starboard side; when both have the wind on the same side, the windward vessel gives way to the leeward vessel.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (Navigation Rules, sailing vessel right-of-way, Rule 12)
